I'm 65 years old, been farming these 16 mu in Quzhou for 35 years. I only finished primary school, so I don't read those extension pamphlets much — I go by what I've seen with my own eyes and what the neighbors do. My son and daughter-in-law help when they can, but my son has a factory job in town, so my wife and I do most of the day-to-day work. This year, money is a bit tight because my grandson is starting school, so I have to watch my spending. But I won't cut back too much on fertilizer — better to waste a little than risk a bad harvest. A bad year hurts more than a good year helps.

My 10 mu of wheat is already in the ground from last October. I plant about 15 kg of improved seed per mu, same as always. I already put down the base fertilizer — about 50 kg of compound fertilizer per mu. Now that it's spring, I'll topdress with urea at jointing, around 10–15 kg per mu. If the wheat looks yellow, I might add a bit more. My neighbor Lao Zhang cut his fertilizer last year and his wheat was short, so I'm not following him there. I'll irrigate three times total — I already did the wintering water, so jointing and heading are left. Well water costs money, but three times is enough.

After wheat harvest in early June, I have maybe five to seven days to get the maize in. That's always a rush. I use hybrid seed, about 3–4 kg per mu. I put compound fertilizer in the hole at planting, then topdress with urea at the big trumpet stage if it doesn't rain. Maize doesn't need as much water as wheat — maybe two irrigations if it's dry. My cousin's business farm uses some fancy planter, but I hire a custom operator or do it myself.

The 4 mu of cotton, I'll plant in late April once it warms up. I use hybrid cotton seed. Cotton is picky — too much fertilizer and it grows leaves instead of bolls. I put down less than wheat, maybe base plus one topdress at flowering. Two irrigations: one at flowering and one when the bolls are setting. The picking takes forever. My wife and I do most of it by hand over many trips, but I might hire two or three days of help when the bolls are bursting.

My 2.1 mu of garlic was also planted last October. Garlic is our cash crop — it makes good money when prices hold, but it needs a lot of work. I save my own cloves for seed when they're good, but sometimes I need to buy some. Garlic needs plenty of food and water. I apply base fertilizer at planting, then topdress again in early spring and once more before the bulbs swell. I'll irrigate four times: planting, winter, spring growth, and bulb expansion. Harvest is in late May, before the wheat comes off. The whole family digs them out because you can't damage the bulbs with machines.

I don't spray pesticides for nothing. If I see weeds, I use herbicide. If I see bugs or disease, I deal with it. Wheat gets a fungicide if it looks sickly. Maize gets herbicide. Cotton needs insecticide for bollworm. Garlic needs some fungicide.

My son helps during harvest and heavy days, but I try not to count on him too much. Family labor does most of the work. I hire a bit when we're overwhelmed, especially for cotton picking and garlic harvest.
